findings.title: Yes: the GitHub/Google Fonts release is plain OFL 1.1, with no Reserved Font Name, and it's forward-licensed
findings.topic: can we add macrons to Atkinson Hyperlegible Next?
findings.html:
The googlefonts/atkinson-hyperlegible-next repo (HEAD 7925f50) ships the standard SIL Open Font License 1.1, copyright "The Atkinson Hyperlegible Next Project Authors", with no Reserved Font Name declared. Under OFL 1.1:

Clause Meaning for us
Permission use, study, copy, modify, redistribute modified copies ✅
1 can't sell the font by itself (bundling with a map product is fine)
2 keep the copyright notice + licence with every copy
3 Reserved Font Names can't be used by modified versions — none are reserved in this release
4 can't use the authors' names to promote our version (acknowledging them is fine)
5 forward licensing: modified versions must be distributed entirely under OFL, and nothing else. Maps and documents made with the font are not bound by this

Sources: S-OFL-ATKINSON-NEXT — OFL.txt in the repo (read directly, C).

findings.title: Caution: the Braille Institute's own download uses a different, OFL-derived licence
findings.topic: can we add macrons to Atkinson Hyperlegible Next?
findings.html: The download from brailleinstitute.org/freefont has historically come with a separate "Atkinson Hyperlegible Font License" — Debian reviewers described it as a modified OFL. One listing of the Next licence names Reserved Font Names "ATKINSON" and "HYPERLEGIBLE". Sources: S-DEBIAN-ATKINSON (D), S-SCANCODE-ATKINSON (C), S-NEXT-RFN (D, secondary listing — not verified against the Braille Institute PDF). Implication: licences attach to the copy you receive. Base any patch on the GitHub OFL sources, and rename the result anyway, so it's compliant whichever text a reader has in mind. Community forks already exist under OFL (e.g. "Atkinson Hyperlegible Pro").

findings.title: The missing Ō/ō only breaks renderers that don't shape text
findings.topic: can we add macrons to Atkinson Hyperlegible Next?
findings.html: HarfBuzz-based renderers (Pillow+raqm here; also browsers and Qt/QGIS, expected but not tested) decompose a missing ō into o + U+0304 and place the macron with the font's mark feature — the official font renders "Taupō" correctly. Renderers that draw one glyph per codepoint show a missing-glyph box instead. MapLibre's glyph PBFs work that way. Evidence: docs/visuals/06-shaping-vs-no-shaping.png (D, measured). Implication: print via QGIS may work today; web maps need the glyphs to exist (patched font, or upstream fix) and glyph PBFs built from that font.

findings.title: The fix is small and mechanical
findings.topic: can we add macrons to Atkinson Hyperlegible Next?
findings.html: Ā and Ū are composites of the base letter + uni0304, centred on the base's bounding box; that rule reproduces their offsets exactly (135, 167). Applying it to O and o gives offsets 179 and 96 (the symmetric o agrees under both centring rules). tools/patch_atkinson_omacron.py does this for static TTFs and renames the result "NZAT Legible Test". Sources: S-OUR-PATCH (D, measured). Known gaps: upright statics only; kerning classes not extended; not reviewed by the type designers.

findings.title: Colour-vision deficiency is common enough to be a primary design constraint
findings.html: About 8% of men have a colour vision impairment (mostly red–green); those affected are slower and less successful at map tasks that depend on colour, and make considerably more colour-identification errors under reduced illumination. Rarer forms affect under ~0.3% of people. Sources: S-JENNY-KELSO-2007 (B/C; reviews Birch 1993 and Cole 2004). Grade: A (prevalence is long-established); B for the map-task effects.

findings.title: Colour vision degrades with age, mostly on the blue–yellow axis
findings.html: In a random sample of 865 adults aged 58–102 with no congenital deficiency, abnormal colour vision rose steeply with age, and most errors were blue–yellow (pastel blue vs purple, yellow vs green/yellow-green). Common age-related eye diseases produce blue–yellow anomalies early. Older observers' tritan-like errors resemble those of younger people tested under dim light, linking ageing and low-light performance. Sources: S-SCHNECK-2014 (B; reported via news summaries — primary paper to be read), S-KNOBLAUCH (B, as cited in S-BARBUR-REVIEW), S-WUERGER-2013 (B). Grade: B. Map implication: pale green vegetation vs pale blue water vs pale grey scree/sand are exactly the confusions this population is prone to.

findings.title: Colour-only distinctions fail; use redundant visual variables
findings.html: The cartographic recommendation is to design for colour-impaired readers by (a) choosing colours that remain distinct under simulation and (b) adding non-colour cues — pattern, line style, shape, size, lightness. Sources: S-JENNY-KELSO-2007. Grade: C (professional guidance grounded in B-grade evidence).

findings.title: The current LINZ web style has measurable CVD weak points
findings.html: From our audit (W4–W7): scrub vs scattered scrub (ΔE <5 for all dichromats), contour vs highway (ΔE ≈6 for everyone), contour vs pipeline (tritan ΔE 3.8), and closed-track status carried by a faint shadow. Sources: our audit (D), using S-MACHADO-2009 simulation and S-SHARMA-2005 ΔE. Grade: D (model output; needs user validation).

findings.title: Under red light, red ink disappears
findings.html: Paper only reflects the wavelengths that hit it. Under a narrow-band red headtorch, red and magenta ink reflect about as much as white paper, so they vanish; blues and greens go dark. Navigators report missing red features on charts under red light, and some military land-navigation training changed red map features to a red-brown for this reason. Sources: physics (reflectance), S-FORUM-REDLIGHT (D, multiple practitioner reports). Grade: D for the anecdotes; the physical mechanism is not in doubt. Our model: contours drop to ~1.4:1 against paper; the closed-track red shadow to ~1.1:1 (W7, W8). Implication: anything safety-relevant (closed tracks, hazards, huts) must be encoded in lightness + shape, never in red hue alone.

findings.title: Dim light worsens colour discrimination for everyone, more for CVD
findings.html: Under reduced illumination, people with colour vision impairment make considerably more colour-identification errors (F-01); older observers' blue–yellow losses resemble those of young people in dim light (F-02). Sources: S-JENNY-KELSO-2007 (B/C, citing Cole 2004), S-BARBUR-REVIEW (B). Implication: design the print palette for dusk/tent light, not a well-lit desk. Lightness contrast is the robust channel.

findings.title: Maps are photocopied, printed mono, and read on e-ink
findings.html: Greyscale reproduction is common (club handouts, SAR briefings, e-ink GPS units, some inReach/e-reader devices). Our audit shows several key pairs with near-identical luminance (W4, W5, W6). Sources: audit (D); S-HARVARD-MONO — practitioner guidance on mono-legible maps (C).

findings.title: Light from NNW reduces terrain-reversal errors compared with NW
findings.html: The relief inversion (terrain reversal) effect makes valleys look like ridges when shading is the main depth cue. A controlled study varying light azimuth found NNW (337.5°), or even N, gave more accurate landform perception than the conventional NW (315°); a replication with a different population broadly confirmed it. The strongest illusion was at 225° (SW). Sources: S-BILAND-2017 (B), S-COLTEKIN-2018 (B). Grade: A– (original + replication). Topo50 today: NW (S-LINZ-GUIDE).

findings.title: NZ-specific twist: northern light is also physically realistic here
findings.html: Cartographic NW lighting is a northern-hemisphere convention that happens to be unrealistic for real sun (which is in the south there). In NZ, the sun is in the north, so NNW/N lighting agrees both with the perceptual research and with what users see on real slopes (sunny north faces). There is no trade-off to make here. Sources: reasoning from F-14 + basic solar geometry (D). Note research suggests the "light from above" prior may be learned from indoor lighting as much as the sun (S-COLTEKIN-2023), so this is a bonus, not the argument.

findings.title: Multidirectional illumination mitigates inversion
findings.html: A multidirectional "sky" illumination model reduced the relief inversion illusion even when the dominant light came from the problematic SW. Sources: S-MULTIDIR-2025 (B, conference abstract). Grade: B– (abstract). Implication: combine NNW primary light with soft multidirectional/sky shading for robustness.

findings.title: Shading interacts with colour and texture
findings.html: Adding colour and texture to shaded relief changes 3D-shape identification; greyscale shading had stronger contrast effects than colour. Overlaying land cover on semi-transparent shading is a common mitigation. Sources: S-COLTEKIN-2019 (B). Implication: test shading under the final vegetation palette, not alone.

findings.title: Contours are a graphical object that must be seen
findings.html: LINZ's web contours are 0.4–0.6 px at 75% opacity, 2.66:1 against white (W3). WCAG 1.4.11 expects 3:1 for graphics needed to understand content (see standards.md). Contour accuracy is ±~10 m and worse in forest/snow (S-LINZ-DD-CONTOUR) — a reason to keep indefinite contours visually distinct (LINZ data carries a definition = indefinite attribute). Sources: audit (D), S-W3C-1411 (C), S-LINZ-DD-CONTOUR (C).

findings.title: Print lines and symbols have practitioner size floors, not a WCAG millimetre
findings.html:
WCAG 1.4.11 (F-20) sets contrast for graphics. It does not set a stroke width. Print size floors come from cartographic practice.

Conversion: 1 pt = 1/72 in ≈ 0.35 mm.

Esri (print, 2008). Type on a printed map should not be smaller than 5 pt. Symbol minimum sizes are about two thirds of the recommended text size. For the 6 pt print floor in F-09, that is about 4 pt ≈ 1.4 mm. The same note uses a 2-minute visual angle as a conservative "can be seen" threshold. At a 300 mm reading distance that angle is about 0.17 mm. The blog has no millimetre table for line width. It is about seeing a mark, not about reading a thin line in a contour mesh. Sources: S-ESRI-MINSIZE (C).

Minnesota map-design guide. Labels: 6 pt minimum, 8 pt preferred (already F-09). Same-colour line weights should differ by at least 1 pt. The worked example is 3 pt / 2 pt / 1 pt (about 1.06 / 0.71 / 0.35 mm). A 0.5 pt step is allowed only if the thinner line is about 20% lighter. Keep line styles to six or fewer. Scale point symbols in 2× size steps. The guide does not prove a laboratory minimum. It treats 1 pt (0.35 mm) as the thin end of a same-colour line family. Sources: S-MN-MAPGUIDE (C).

USGS US Topo (1:24,000), not 1:50,000. These are product specs for standard-vision maps, not a low-vision floor. StreamRiver perennial and intermittent strokes are 0.80–1.00 pt (0.28–0.35 mm). Index contours are 0.504 pt (0.18 mm). Intermediate contours are 0.216 pt (0.08 mm). Paper millimetres do not double when scale halves. Use the millimetre figures as a same-paper check, not as a scale-up. Sources: S-USGS-SPECS (C).

This sheet today (BX24, millimetres on paper).

Mark Width or size In points Against the floors
Stock stream 0.10 mm 0.28 pt Below USGS stream stroke and MN 1 pt
Accessible river and canal (log 0071) 0.25 mm 0.71 pt Above the 0.17 mm visual angle. Under the USGS stream stroke
Accessible drain (log 0071) 0.15 mm 0.43 pt One MN 1 pt step thinner would be 0 mm, so the step is smaller
Index contour 0.35 mm 1.0 pt Matches MN 1 pt
Intermediate contour fill 0.12 mm 0.34 pt USGS-thin; stays recessive (OQ-09)
Scrub plant third_arc 1.4 mm 4.0 pt Matches Esri 2/3 of 6 pt
Closed-track × 0.5 mm 1.4 pt Line-on-line mark, not an area symbol. G1 locked

Implication: A single line floor does not work on this sheet (log 0071). One 0.35 mm width on every blue line made drains, pond rims and coastline look like rivers. MN treats 1 pt as the thin end of a family, so each class needs its own step. Rivers are 0.25 mm and drains 0.15 mm. Polygon outlines, coastline, shelterbelt, and grid keep stock widths in the darker inks. Scrub marks use the ~1.4 mm symbol size. Do not copy USGS contour millimetres as a low-vision floor.

Grade: C (practitioner guidance).

findings.title: NZ government web must meet WCAG 2.2 AA, with a maps exception
findings.html: The NZ Government Web Accessibility Standard 1.2 (effective 17 March 2025) requires WCAG 2.2 Level AA, with listed exceptions including complex visual maps; the draft modified requirement was that data presented in complex visual maps be published in open, machine-readable formats via data.govt.nz. A Digital Accessibility Standard is being developed to extend beyond websites. Sources: S-NZ-WAS-1.2 (C), S-NZ-WAS-DRAFT (C). Implication: a topo map is likely "exempt", but the exemption is about equivalent data, not permission to be hard to read. LINZ already publishes the data openly, so our job is purely legibility. We should still adopt WCAG ratios as design targets because they encode real low-vision limits.

findings.title: WCAG ratios we will use as targets
findings.html:
• Text: 4.5:1 (1.4.3 AA); 3:1 for large text.
  • Graphical objects needed for understanding: 3:1 against adjacent colours (1.4.11). W3C's own guidance treats each line/shape in a chart as a graphical object; where many adjacent colours make 3:1 impossible, giving areas a contrasting border is a common practitioner fix.
  • Use of colour (1.4.1): colour must not be the only means of conveying information. Sources: S-W3C-1411 (C), W3C WAI-IG thread (D).

findings.title: Macrons are mandatory on official names, and the set is growing
findings.html: Ngā Pou Taunaha o Aotearoa (NZ Geographic Board) made 824 Māori place names official in 2019, adding macrons to about 300 (e.g. Taupō). Further batches since (e.g. 541 Auckland names, 194 gaining macrons). Once official, names must be used on maps, signs, websites and databases. Sources: S-NZGB-2019 (C), S-LINZ-NZGB-AUCK (C). Grade: C (statutory). Map implication: any typeface we choose must render all ten macron vowels in every weight/style used, in both the print toolchain and the MapLibre glyph PBFs. This is a hard gate, not a preference.

findings.title: Long names stress the label system
findings.html: Official names include very long single words (the 85-character hill name in Hawke's Bay) and hyphenated compounds (e.g. Te Horohoroinga-o-ngā-ringa-o- Kahumatamomoe). Increased letter-spacing (F-07) makes these longer still. Sources: S-NZGB-2019, LINZ NZGB notices (C). Implication: letter-spacing needs a ceiling, and line-breaking at hyphens/spaces should be allowed (text-max-width).

findings.title: Track symbology is the most criticised part of Topo50
findings.html: Topo50 tracks are all black, symbolised much as in 1977, with three main types (vehicle, foot, poled route) and a closed-route sign, and no indication of public vs private access. A 2020 petition asked LINZ and the Walking Access Commission to redesign them; the Commission's online map has had to overlay coloured lines on the black tracks as a stop-gap. Sources: S-MCDONALD-2020 (D — advocacy document, but detailed and well-referenced).

findings.title: Access status is not in the topo data
findings.html: Access (public/private, gazetted walkway, DOC track) comes from other datasets (Walking Access Commission, DOC). Showing it is a data question as much as a design one, and is out of scope for a pure re-style of LINZ layers — but the symbology should leave room for it (e.g. a reserved channel such as casing colour/pattern). Sources: S-MCDONALD-2020.

findings.title: Italics reduce readability for dyslexic readers; roman sans-serif helps
findings.html: In an eye-tracking study (48 participants with dyslexia, 12 fonts), sans-serif, monospaced and roman (upright) styles significantly improved reading performance over serif, proportional and italic styles. Arial Italic in particular decreased readability. A later journal version found fonts that helped dyslexic readers were equally good for non-dyslexic readers. Sources: S-RELLO-2013 (B), S-RELLO-2016 (B). Grade: B (single lab; consistent across two publications).

findings.title: "Dyslexia fonts" do not help
findings.html: Dyslexie did not improve speed or accuracy for 170 children with dyslexia (Exp. 1) or for 102 dyslexic + 45 typical readers (Exp. 2); most preferred Arial. OpenDyslexic showed no improvement in rate or accuracy either. Sources: S-KUSTER-2018 (B), S-WERY-2017 (B), S-RELLO-2016 (B). Grade: A (multiple independent studies agree). Map implication: don't adopt a novelty "dyslexia font". Choose a well-designed roman sans-serif.

findings.title: Extra letter spacing helps dyslexic readers (and rescues bad fonts)
findings.html: Increased inter-letter spacing improved reading accuracy (≈2×) and speed (≈20%) for dyslexic children in Italian and French, with no gain for typical readers; the poorest readers benefited most. The proposed mechanism is crowding — dyslexic readers are abnormally affected by flanking letters. A follow-up found spacing, not font, drove the benefit, and that spacing removed the penalty of italic and decorative fonts. Sources: S-ZORZI-2012 (B), S-SPACING-2018 (B). Grade: A– (two studies, different labs; children, not adults). Map implication: map labels are short, isolated words — but they are heavily crowded by linework. Tracking (letter-spacing) and halos both attack crowding. MapLibre exposes text-letter-spacing.

findings.title: Cartographic convention puts water names in italic
findings.html: Long-standing guidance labels water features in blue italic; area features in spaced capitals. The LINZ web style follows this (36 of 68 label layers italic, all water labels italic). Sources: S-AXIS-LABELING (C), S-USGS-SPECS (C), audit (D). Tension with F-05: the convention and the dyslexia evidence point in opposite directions. Colour + case/weight can carry the "this is water" signal without italics. Topo50 (log 0059): on BX24, italic marks natural features, not only water. All 66 water labels, 230 of 231 spot heights and 69 other names (peaks, passes, heads, points, rocks, islands, valleys, saddles, forest areas) are italic. Names with a landform word that are settlements, localities, huts or roads are upright (Gebbies Valley, Heathcote Valley, Mount Pleasant). Removing italic removes the natural-versus-cultural cue, so another cue must carry it.

findings.title: Minimum label sizes and size steps
findings.html: Practitioner guidance converges on ~6 pt as an absolute print minimum (8 pt preferred), ~9–10 px on screen, and size differences under ~15% not being noticed by readers — so hierarchy steps should be bigger than that. x-height matters as much as point size at small sizes. Sources: S-COLORADO-TYPO (C), S-AXIS-LABELING (C), S-ESRI-MINSIZE (C), S-MN-MAPGUIDE (C). Grade: C.

findings.title: Atkinson Hyperlegible targets character confusions; evidence is thin and it can't yet set all Māori names
findings.html: Designed by the Braille Institute (2019; Next 2025) to differentiate confusable characters (I/l/1, O/0, B/8). Evidence base is mostly the designers' own user testing, not independent peer-reviewed studies. Our check: Atkinson Hyperlegible Next v2.001 (google/fonts, upstream commit 7925f50) lacks precomposed Ō/ō (U+014C/U+014D) while having the other macron vowels. It does have a combining macron and mark positioning, but MapLibre's glyph rendering doesn't do OpenType mark positioning, so Taupō, Ōtautahi, Ōpōtiki, Ōamaru would break on the web. Refined in log 0018 (F-28): shaping renderers (HarfBuzz) do render these correctly with the official font; only per-codepoint renderers like MapLibre break. Licence permits patching (F-26). Sources: S-ATKINSON (C/D), S-ATKINSON-NEXT (C), tools/font_check.py (D). Grade: D (design rationale) / measured fact for glyph coverage.

findings.title: Topo50's own labels are mostly condensed italic at 5.5–6.5 pt
findings.html: In the carto_text sample shipped with LINZ's production pipeline, 300 of 445 labels (67%) are italic, 288 of them Narrow (condensed) italic; 394 are set at 5.5–6.5 pt. Fonts are Nimbus Sans LINZ (a Helvetica-metric URW font, renamed by LINZ) standing in for the legacy "ATTriumMou" faces; all ten macron vowels are present. Condensed + italic + small is the combination the dyslexia research (F-05, F-07) and crowding mechanism point against. Sources: S-LINZ-TOPO-QGIS, S-LINZ-TOPO-SYSTEM (C); S-OUR-QGIS-ANALYSIS (D). Caveat: a test-area sample, not nationwide. Labels are data-defined, so the fix is an override in the QML (style expression), not a data edit. Meaning (log 0059): the italic rows are not random. They mark the natural-feature class (F-08). The data has no feature-class column, so the style value is the only class signal a label override can read.

findings.title: Open Sans (LINZ's current face) is already a reasonable choice
findings.html:
Open Sans has full macron coverage and a large x-height (0.535 em vs 0.496 for Atkinson Next, 0.478 for Source Sans 3). Noto Sans is near-identical in metrics with far wider coverage. The issue in the current style is not the family; it's the italics, contrast and spacing. Sources: tools/font_check.py output (D, measured).

recommendations.title: Encode anything safety-relevant in lightness and shape; use hue only as a redundant cue
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-01, F-02, F-03, F-21, F-22, F-23 · Best evidence: A/B Why: CVD affects ~8% of men; ageing adds blue–yellow losses; dim light and red headtorches remove hue information for everyone. Lightness and shape survive all of these. Met when: every pair in the must-distinguish list either reaches ≥3:1 luminance contrast in the greyscale model or differs in pattern/shape, and the same holds in the red-light model. A line, glyph or label that sits on a fill is measured against that fill as well as against paper (for example index contour on scrub, stream on scrub).

recommendations.title: Keep the familiar colour grammar; change values within it
recommendations.html: Rests on: S-LINZ-GUIDE (C), F-24 · Provisional Why: Blue = water, brown = relief, green = vegetation, black = culture is an international convention that SAR teams, trampers and the Defence Force are trained on. The audit shows most problems are lightness problems inside that grammar, not wrong hues. Met when: a Topo50 user can read the new style without consulting the legend for the core classes. (Test, see R-16.)

recommendations.title: Light relief shading from NNW (337.5°), with a soft multidirectional component
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-14, F-15, F-16, F-17, S-MAPLIBRE-2320 · Best evidence: A– Change from today: Topo50 uses NW (315°). Why: Replicated studies show fewer terrain-reversal errors with NNW than NW. In the southern hemisphere this is also where the real sun is. Met when: shaded relief generated at 337.5°, blended with a multidirectional/sky layer; evaluated on both Alpine and lowland sheets.

recommendations.title: Contours that stay visible: strong index lines, recessive intermediates
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-18, F-20, F-31, W3, W5, W6, palette v0 · Best evidence: C (WCAG) + D (audit) Starting values: index #7A5542 at alpha 0.85, intermediate #B08872 at alpha 0.5 (hexes from log 0050; alpha from logs 0053 and 0054). Lightness of the hexes is unchanged. Stroke alpha recedes the 20 m mesh on dense slopes (OQ-09). Web widths: intermediate ≥1 px, index ≥1.5 px at z13+ (provisional). Print widths: index 0.35 mm matches the F-31 1 pt figure. Intermediate fill stays 0.12 mm with a 0.2 mm casing (OQ-09). Rivers are 0.25 mm and drains 0.15 mm, so water stays under the index line (log 0071). Confirm on a steep sheet. Also: draw definition = indefinite contours dashed, so reduced accuracy in forest/snow is visible. Met when: index contours ≥3:1 vs paper (grey and red); ΔE ≥10 vs highways and pipelines under all simulated dichromacies. Intermediate strokes may fall below 3:1.

recommendations.title: No italics for map labels
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-05, F-08, F-30 · Best evidence: B Change from today: 33 of 63 web label layers are italic, including all water names. Why: Italic styles measurably slowed dyslexic readers; the italic-water convention is a tradition, not a legibility finding. Carry "this is water" with colour (≥4.5:1, R-07) and, if needed, a weight or tracking difference. In Topo50, italic also marks natural features (F-08, log 0059). That class needs its own non-italic cue too. Met when: zero italic faces in the style, including text drawn as symbols (contour-number FontMarkers); and natural-feature names differ from cultural names by a non-italic cue (colour, weight or case) on the full grid.

recommendations.title: Use a roman, humanist sans with a large x-height and complete macron coverage; do not use "dyslexia fonts"
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-06, F-10, F-11, F-12 · Best evidence: A (dyslexia fonts don't help); measured (coverage) Now: keep Open Sans (or Noto Sans, near-identical metrics, broader coverage). Both have all ten macron vowels and x-height ≈0.535 em. Later: adopt Atkinson Hyperlegible Next once Ō/ō exist in a build we can make glyph PBFs from (F-26 – F-29). Preferred route: upstream PR adding two composites (docs/upstream/). Interim route: our renamed OFL patch (tools/patch_atkinson_omacron.py). It's designed to separate I/l/1 and O/0 (docs/visuals/05), which matters for grid references and trig IDs. Print via a shaping renderer (QGIS) may work with the official font already (F-28). QGIS fork (log 0024): the accessible sheet uses that interim patch now (upright statics). The stock sheet keeps Nimbus Sans LINZ. The web vector style stays on Open Sans until glyph PBFs exist. Met when: tools/font_check.py reports full macron coverage for every face in the style (hard gate, F-12).

recommendations.title: All label text ≥4.5:1 against an opaque halo
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-20, W1 · Best evidence: C Change: water labels #008CCC → #005C8F (3.3:1 → 6.2:1); contour labels and grey POI labels darkened; halos fully opaque. Met when: the text-contrast table in the audit has no ⚠️/❌ rows (except shield-on-icon false positives, documented).

recommendations.title: Add modest positive letter-spacing, and allow long names to wrap
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-07, F-13 · Best evidence: A– for continuous reading; transfer to map labels unproven (OQ-06). Starting values: +0.04–0.08 em tracking on point/area labels; halos retained; text-max-width so hyphenated Māori names break at hyphens. Met when: A/B tested with dyslexic readers on label-finding tasks.

recommendations.title: Label size floor and hierarchy steps
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-09 · Best evidence: C Values: print ≥7 pt default, 6 pt absolute floor (spot heights only); web ≥10 px (≥11 px for place names); adjacent hierarchy levels differ by ≥20%. Spot heights are their own rank, below locality names. Met when: every label is at or above its floor; spot heights, locality names and place names each differ from the next rank by ≥20%; and on the full grid no label's glyphs touch another label's glyphs, and each name sits nearer its own feature than any other feature of the same kind.

recommendations.title: Vegetation classes that affect travel get pattern as well as tint
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-02, F-04, palette v0 · Best evidence: B + D Change: scrub #A3CC90; scattered scrub #E0EDD8 plus stipple. Water keeps its blue shoreline line. Why: v0 showed colour alone can't separate pale fills in greyscale.

recommendations.title: Closed tracks, hazards and historic sites: meaning in shape, not red
recommendations.html: Print evidence (log 0019, P2): in printed Topo50, a closed track differs from a foot track only by gap length (dash 24/gap 12 vs 23/24). This applies to print as much as web. Rests on: F-21, W7, palette v0 · Best evidence: D (mechanism certain) Change: closed tracks get a dark casing with cross-bars; historic sites get a distinct glyph with dark-ink labels. Met when: red-light model ≥3:1 vs paper for all safety-relevant marks, and no new or changed symbol can be read as another legend symbol (railway, embankment, cutting, cliff, fence, boundary) where tracks run close together on the full grid.

recommendations.title: Reserve a symbol channel for track access status
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-24, F-25 · Provisional Why: the most-requested change from the tramping community needs data we don't have; leave a casing/colour channel unused so it can be added without redesign. Met when: tools/style-topo50.json records a track-access casing/colour channel that the QGIS apply step and the vector build do not paint.

recommendations.title: Publish three variants from one source
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-01, F-02, F-23 · Best evidence: B Full colour (web + print), greyscale-safe print (F-23), and a high-contrast web variant for low-vision users.

recommendations.title: Run the audit in CI on every style change
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-04, S-OUR-AUDIT-WEB · Best evidence: D palette_audit.py and font_check.py against the style; fail on new ❌ rows. Pair colours that live in tools/style-topo50.json are resolved from that file. Makes regressions visible and keeps the evidence chain alive.

recommendations.title: Publish the raster style as a MapLibre style on Shortbread tiles
recommendations.html: Rests on: S-LINZ-BASEMAPS-CONFIG, S-LINZ-BASEMAPS-STYLING · Best evidence: C The vector style is the raster style in tools/style-topo50.json. tools/build_style.py writes owned paint onto the layer catalog in upstream/linz-topographic-v2.json. Layers the style file does not name keep LINZ paint. The vector face stays Open Sans until macron glyph PBFs exist. Met when: the built MapLibre style is generated from that catalog and that style file, and P in tools/build_style.py holds no colour hex.

recommendations.title: Validate with real users before calling anything "accessible"
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-04, F-06, F-14 · Best evidence: A (that model results need validation is a method point) Grade D model results must be confirmed. Minimum: (a) CVD readers, (b) dyslexic readers, (c) readers 60+, (d) LandSAR / tramping club members familiar with Topo50. Tasks: identify landform (ridge vs valley), follow a track, find a named feature, judge vegetation, read a grid reference — on paper under daylight, dusk, and red headtorch, and on a phone.

recommendations.title: Print-specific fixes found in the Topo50 legend
recommendations.html: Rests on: P1–P9 (current-state/topo50-print.md), F-21, F-23 · Best evidence: measured (D) + C - Give hot and cold springs different glyphs, not just different inks (P3: 1.13:1 in greyscale). Topo50 already does this well for hot spring vs fumarole (× vs ⊗) — extend the same idea. - Separate native forest from scrub by a larger lightness step or a texture (P5: ΔE 4.8, 1.1:1 greyscale). This changes route choice. - Keep scattered scrub as a pattern (P6) — print got this right; the web style should match (R-10 does). - Apply R-05 to contour labels and spot heights, which are italic in print (P8). - Don't use the red-orange ink alone for anything that must be read under a red headtorch (P7).

recommendations.title: Make Topo50 itself more accessible: fork LINZ's QGIS symbology and re-render
recommendations.html: Rests on: F-30, S-LINZ-RASTER-STYLE, S-LINZ-TOPO-QGIS, S-LINZ-TOPO-SYSTEM · Best evidence: C Why: the intended starting point, topo-raster-gridded, is pre-rendered Topo50 imagery. A MapLibre style can only adjust it globally (brightness, contrast, saturation, hue) and its client hillshade; it cannot recolour contours, change fonts or remove italics. The cartography lives in LINZ's MIT-licensed topographic-qgis project, rendered by the containerised pipeline in topographic-system. Forking the QMLs and re-rendering yields both accessible raster tiles and print (R-13) from one source. Met when: an accessible QML set renders at least one Topo50 sheet through LINZ's map container, and the R-01/R-05/R-07/R-11/R-17 gates pass on it. Fonts: the stock sheet keeps unmodified Nimbus Sans LINZ (AGPL-3.0; the exemption covers embedding those files in that PDF). The accessible sheet swaps labels to Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, upright, with Ō/ō added by the OFL patch (log 0024, R-06). This project does not modify the Nimbus files.
